blocks.text: Knowing what a linked list is matters less than knowing **when to reach for one**. In everyday code an array (or a growable list) is the right default. A linked list wins in a few specific situations — and interviews love those situations.

items: **You add or remove at the front a lot.** A stack, a queue, an undo history: work happens at the ends, and a list does it in O(1) with no shifting.

**You insert or delete in the middle at a spot you already hold.** If you have a pointer to the node, splicing a new node in (or one out) is O(1). A text editor's buffer or an LRU cache does exactly this.
**The size changes a lot and you can't predict it.** Nodes are allocated one at a time; there's no capacity to outgrow and no big copy.
**You only ever walk through in order.** If you always start at the beginning and go forward, losing random access costs you nothing.
**You need the ith element directly.** Reading index i means walking i arrows. Binary search, which jumps to the middle again and again, becomes pointless.
**Memory is tight.** Every node carries a pointer, sometimes doubling the memory used.
**You scan big collections over and over.** Arrays sit together in memory, so the CPU's cache streams them quickly; scattered nodes are much slower to walk in practice.

blocks.alt: A decision flow. Do you need to read elements by index? Yes leads to: use an array. No leads to: do you insert or delete at the front, or at a node you already hold? Yes leads to: a linked list is a great fit. No leads to: use an array, it is simpler and faster to scan.

blocks.text: Where linked lists hide in real software

blocks.alt: Four real uses of linked lists: a music playlist where each song points to the next; browser history with back and forward; an undo stack in an editor; and a hash table whose buckets are short linked lists of colliding keys.

items: **Undo / redo** and **browser back/forward**: a (doubly) linked list of states.
**Music playlists and image carousels**: "next" and "previous" are just arrows; a circular list loops forever.
**Hash tables**: keys that collide in the same bucket are kept in a short linked list ("chaining").
**LRU caches** (used by browsers, databases and CDNs): a doubly linked list keeps items in order of use, so moving one to the front is O(1).
**Other data structures**: stacks, queues and graph adjacency lists are often built from linked nodes.
Default to an **array**; reach for a **linked list** when you mostly insert and delete at the ends, or at nodes you already hold.
Never use a linked list when you need **indexing** or **binary search**.
Many famous structures — LRU caches, hash table buckets, queues — are linked lists inside.
